{{smaller block|O I that wasted time to ''tend upon'' her,
To compass her with sweet observances.
{{right|''Tennyson'', Geraint.}}}}

2†. To be in waiting; be ready for service; attend.

{{smaller block|The associates ''tend'', and everything is bent
For England. {{right|''Shak.'', Hamlet, iv. 3. 47.}}}}

3†. To be attentive; listen.

{{smaller block|''Tend'' to the master's whistle. {{right|''Shak.'', Tempest, i. 1. 8.}}}}

'''tend<sup>3</sup>'''†, ''v. t.'' See ''tind.''

'''tend<sup>4</sup>'''†. Obsolete past participle of ''teen<sup>1</sup>''.

'''tendable'''† (ten′da̤-bl), ''a.'' [< ''tend<sup>2</sup>'' + ''-able.''] Attentive.

{{smaller block|A ''tendable'' [var. ''plyaunt''] seruaunt standeth in fauour.
{{right|''Hugh Rhodes'', quoted in Babees Book (E. E. T. S.), p. lxxxii.}}}}

'''tendance''' (ten′da̤ns), ''n.'' [Also sometimes ''tendence;'' by apheresis from ''attendance;'' cf. ''tend<sup>2</sup>'' for ''attend.''] 1†. Expectant waiting; expectancy.

{{smaller block|Unhappie wight, borne to desastrous end,
That doth his life in so long ''tendance'' spend!
{{right|''Spenser'', Mother Hub. Tale, l. 908.}}}}

2. Persons waiting or in attendance.

{{smaller block|All those which were his fellows but of late . . .
Follow his strides, his lobbies fill with ''tendance'',
Rain sacrificial whisperings in his ear.
{{right|''Shak.'', T. of A., i. 1. 80.}}}}

3. Attendance; the work or art of tending or caring for some person or thing; attention; care; watchful supervision or care.

{{smaller block|Good Host, such ''tendence'' as you would expect
From your own children if yourself were sick,
Let this old Man find at your hands.
{{right|''Wordsworth'', The Borderers, i.}}}}

akin to ''tenuis'', thin, fine: see ''thin''.] '''I.''' ''a.'' '''1†.''' Thin; slender; attenuated; fine: literally or figuratively.

{{smaller block|The happes over mannes hede
Ben honge with a ''tender'' threde.
{{right|''Gower'', Conf. Amant., vi.}}
'Midst this was heard the shrill and ''tender'' cry
Of well-pleased ghosts, which in the storm did fly.
{{right|''Dryden'', Tyrannic Love, i. 1.}}}}

'''2.''' Of fine or delicate quality; delicate; fine; soft: as, a ''tender'' glow of color.

{{smaller block|This set so many artists on worke, that they soone ariv'd to y<sup>t</sup> perfection it is since come, emulating the ''tenderest'' miniatures. {{right|''Evelyn'', Diary, March 13, 1661.}}
Late, in a flood of ''tender'' light,
She floated through the ethereal blue.
{{right|''Bryant'', The Waning Moon.}}
I treasure in secret some long fine hair
Of ''tenderest'' brown. {{right|''Lowell'', Wind-Harp.}}}}

'''3†.''' Soft; thin; watery.

{{smaller block|We saw
My rider . . .
Vault o'er his mare into a ''tender'' slough.
{{right|''Shirley'', Hyde Park, iv. 3.}}}}

'''4.''' Delicate to the touch, or yielding readily to the action of a cutting instrument or to a blow; not tough or hard; especially, soft and easily masticated: as, ''tender'' meat.

{{smaller block|Floriz ne let for ne feo
To finden al that neod beo,
Of fless of fiss, of ''tendre'' bred,
Of whit win and eke red.
{{right|''King Horn'' (E. E. T. S.), p. 52.}}
We had some beef-steak, not so ''tender'' as it might have been, some of the potatoes, some cheese.
{{right|''R. L. Stevenson'', Inland Voyage, p. 73.}}}}

{{RunningHeader|tend|6229|tender}}{{smaller block|It is ordered at Common Counsell that the new Mayor ''tenne'' the old Mayor at his owne house, and goe home with the sword before him afterward. {{right|''English Gilds'' (E. E. T. S.), p. 418.}}}} {{smaller block|And flaming ministers to watch and ''tend'' Their earthly charge. {{right|''Milton'', P. L., ix. 156.}}}} '''2.''' To look after; take care of; have the charge, care, or supervision of: as, to ''tend'' a machine; to ''tend'' a flock; to ''tend'' a sick person. {{smaller block|The Boy of whom I speak In summer ''tended'' cattle on the hills. {{right|''Wordsworth'', Excursion, i.}}}} {{smaller block|I would fain stay and help thee ''tend'' him! {{right|''M. Arnold'', Empedocles on Etna.}}}} {{smaller block|The mother . . . sat at the foot of the bed and ''tended'' Annie's baby. {{right|''The Atlantic'', XLIX. 54.}}}} '''3†.''' To be attentive to; attend to; be mindful of; mind. {{smaller block|Unsuck'd of lamb or kid that ''tend'' their play. {{right|''Milton'', P. L., ix. 583.}}}} '''4.''' To wait upon so as to execute; be prepared to perform. [Rare.] {{smaller block|By all the stars that ''tend'' thy bidding. {{right|''Keats.''}}}} '''5.''' ''Naut.'', to watch, as a vessel at anchor, at the turn of tides, and cast her by the helm, and by some sail if necessary, so as to keep turns out of her cable. ='''Syn.''' {{smaller|1 and 2. To keep, protect, nurse.}} '''II.''' ''intrans.'' '''1.''' To attend; wait as an attendant or servant: with ''on'' or ''upon''. {{smaller block|Was he not companion with the riotous knights That ''tend upon'' my father? {{right|''Shak.'', Lear, ii. 1. 96.}} O I that wasted time to ''tend upon'' her, To compass her with sweet observances. {{right|''Tennyson'', Geraint.}}}} 2†. To be in waiting; be ready for service; attend. {{smaller block|The associates ''tend'', and everything is bent For England. {{right|''Shak.'', Hamlet, iv. 3. 47.}}}} 3†. To be attentive; listen. {{smaller block|''Tend'' to the master's whistle. {{right|''Shak.'', Tempest, i. 1. 8.}}}} '''tend3'''†, ''v. t.'' See ''tind.'' '''tend4'''†. Obsolete past participle of ''teen1''. '''tendable'''† (ten′da̤-bl), ''a.'' [< ''tend2'' + ''-able.''] Attentive. {{smaller block|A ''tendable'' [var. ''plyaunt''] seruaunt standeth in fauour. {{right|''Hugh Rhodes'', quoted in Babees Book (E. E. T. S.), p. lxxxii.}}}} '''tendance''' (ten′da̤ns), ''n.'' [Also sometimes ''tendence;'' by apheresis from ''attendance;'' cf. ''tend2'' for ''attend.''] 1†. Expectant waiting; expectancy. {{smaller block|Unhappie wight, borne to desastrous end, That doth his life in so long ''tendance'' spend! {{right|''Spenser'', Mother Hub. Tale, l. 908.}}}} 2. Persons waiting or in attendance. {{smaller block|All those which were his fellows but of late . . . Follow his strides, his lobbies fill with ''tendance'', Rain sacrificial whisperings in his ear. {{right|''Shak.'', T. of A., i. 1. 80.}}}} 3. Attendance; the work or art of tending or caring for some person or thing; attention; care; watchful supervision or care. {{smaller block|Good Host, such ''tendence'' as you would expect From your own children if yourself were sick, Let this old Man find at your hands. {{right|''Wordsworth'', The Borderers, i.}}}} '''tendant†''' (ten′dant), ''n.'' [By apheresis from ''attendant.''] An attendant. {{smaller block|His ''tendants'' round about
Him, fainting, falling, carried in with care. {{right|''Vicars'', tr. of Virgil, 1632. (''Nares.'')}}}} '''tendence1''' (ten′dens), ''n.'' [< F. ''tendance'' = Sp. Pg. ''tendencia'' = It. ''tendenza'', < ML. as if *''tendentia'', < L. ''tenden(t-)s'', ppr. of ''tendere'', stretch, extend: see ''tend''1.] Tendency. [Rare.] {{smaller block|He freely moves and acts according to his most natural ''tendence'' and inclination. {{right|''J. Scott'', Christian Life, i. 1.}}}} '''tendence2''' (ten′dens), ''n.'' Same as ''tendance.'' '''tendency''' (ten′dẹn-si), ''n.'' [As ''tendence''1 (see ''-cy'').] Movement, or inclination to move, in some particular direction or toward some end or purpose; bent, leaning, or inclination toward some object, effect, or result; inclining or contributing influence. {{smaller block|The tenderest mother could not have been more anxious and careful as to the religious ''tendency'' of any books we read. {{right|''Lady Holland'', Sydney Smith, vi.}}}} {{smaller block|''Tendency'' is the ideal summation of the statical conditions which tend to a dynamical result; or, to express it less technically, it is one gathering up into a picture of all the events which we foresee will succeed each other when the organism is set going, and of the final result. {{right|''G. H. Lewes'', Probs. of Life and Mind, I. ii. § 38.}}}} {{smaller block|Everywhere the history of religion betrays a ''tendency'' to enthusiasm. {{right|''Emerson'', Essays, 1st ser., p. 256.}}}} {{smaller block|='''Syn.''' ''Propensity, Inclination'', etc. (see ''bent''1), drift, direction, bearing.}} '''tender1''' (ten′dėr), ''a.'' and ''n.'' [< ME. ''tender'', ''tendre'', < OF. (and F.) ''tendre'' = Pr. ''tenre'', ''tendre'' = Sp. ''tierno'' = Pg. ''tenro'' = It. ''tenero'', < L. ''tener'', soft, delicate, tender, of tender age, young; akin to ''tenuis'', thin, fine: see ''thin''.] '''I.''' ''a.'' '''1†.''' Thin; slender; attenuated; fine: literally or figuratively. {{smaller block|The happes over mannes hede Ben honge with a ''tender'' threde. {{right|''Gower'', Conf. Amant., vi.}} 'Midst this was heard the shrill and ''tender'' cry Of well-pleased ghosts, which in the storm did fly. {{right|''Dryden'', Tyrannic Love, i. 1.}}}} '''2.''' Of fine or delicate quality; delicate; fine; soft: as, a ''tender'' glow of color. {{smaller block|This set so many artists on worke, that they soone ariv'd to yt perfection it is since come, emulating the ''tenderest'' miniatures. {{right|''Evelyn'', Diary, March 13, 1661.}} Late, in a flood of ''tender'' light, She floated through the ethereal blue. {{right|''Bryant'', The Waning Moon.}} I treasure in secret some long fine hair Of ''tenderest'' brown. {{right|''Lowell'', Wind-Harp.}}}} '''3†.''' Soft; thin; watery. {{smaller block|We saw My rider . . . Vault o'er his mare into a ''tender'' slough. {{right|''Shirley'', Hyde Park, iv. 3.}}}} '''4.''' Delicate to the touch, or yielding readily to the action of a cutting instrument or to a blow; not tough or hard; especially, soft and easily masticated: as, ''tender'' meat. {{smaller block|Floriz ne let for ne feo To finden al that neod beo, Of fless of fiss, of ''tendre'' bred, Of whit win and eke red. {{right|''King Horn'' (E. E. T. S.), p. 52.}} We had some beef-steak, not so ''tender'' as it might have been, some of the potatoes, some cheese. {{right|''R. L. Stevenson'', Inland Voyage, p. 73.}}}} 5. Soft; impressible; susceptible; sensitive; compassionate; easily touched, affected, or influenced: as, a ''tender'' heart. {{smaller block|As you have pity, stop those ''tender'' ears From his enchanting voice. {{right|''Beau. and Fl.'', King and No King, ii. 1.}}}} {{smaller block|He was, above many, ''tender'' of sin. {{right|''Bunyan'', Pilgrim's Progress, ii.}}}} {{smaller block|In the way to our lodging we met a messenger from the countess of Falchensteyn, a pretty young ''tender'' man, near to the kingdom, who saluted us in her name with much love. {{right|''Penn'', Travels in Holland, etc.}}}} {{smaller block|To each his sufferings; all are men Condemned alike to groan; The ''tender'' for another's pain, The unfeeling for his own. {{right|''Gray'', On a Distant Prospect of Eton College.}}}} 6. Expressing sensitive feeling; expressing the gentle emotions, as love or pity, especially the former; kindly; loving; affectionate; fond. {{smaller block|You have show'd a ''tender'' fatherly regard. {{right|''Shak.'', T. of the S., ii. 1. 288.}}}} {{smaller block|Her wide gray eyes Made ''tenderer'' with those thronging memories. {{right|''William Morris'', Earthly Paradise, II. 295.}}}} {{smaller block|I desired him to repeat to me the translation he had made of some ''tender'' verses in Theocritus. {{right|''Steele'', Tatler, No. 207.}}}} {{smaller block|That Number Five foresaw from the first that any ''tenderer'' feeling than that of friendship would intrude itself between them I do not believe. {{right|''O. W. Holmes'', The Atlantic, LXVI. 665.}}}} 7. Delicate in constitution, consistency, texture, etc.; fragile; easily injured, broken, or bruised. {{smaller block|I know how ''tender'' reputation is,
And with what guards it ought to be preserv'd, lady. {{right|''Fletcher'', Rule a Wife, i. 1.}}}} {{smaller block|And certainly, if the air was the cause of the elasticity of springs, as some have imagined, it would have been perceived in so ''tender'' a movement as a pocket watch, lying under the perpetual influence of two springs. {{right|''W. Derham'', in Ellis's Lit. Letters, p. 317.}}}} {{smaller block|Where'er the ''tender'' grass was leading
Its earliest green along the lane. {{right|''Wordsworth'', Peter Bell.}}}} '''8.''' Delicate as regards health; weakly. [Scotch.] {{smaller block|I am sure I wad hae answered for her as my ain daughter; but, wae 's my heart, I had been ''tender'' a' the simmer, and scarce ower the door o' my room for twal weeks. {{right|''Scott'', Heart of Mid-Lothian, v.}}}} '''9.''' Very sensitive to impression; very susceptible of any sensation or emotion; easily pained. {{smaller block|What art thou call'st me from my holy rites,
And with the fearèd name of death affrights
My ''tender'' ears? {{right|''Fletcher'', Faithful Shepherdess, iv. 2.}}}} '''10.''' Not strong; not hardy; not able to endure hardship or rough treatment; delicate; weak. {{smaller block|But longe ne myght endure the cristin, for yet the childeren were ''tendre'' and grene, so that thei moste nede remeve a-brode in to the feilde, and in short tyme thei sholde haue hadde grete losse. {{right|''Merlin'' (E. E. T. S.), ii. 287.}}}} {{smaller block|My lord knoweth that the children are ''tender''. {{right|Gen. xxxiii. 13.}}}} {{smaller block|The ''tender'' and delicate woman among you. {{right|Deut. xxviii. 56.}} So far beneath your soft and ''tender'' breeding. {{right|''Shak.'', T. N., v. 1. 331.}}}} {{smaller block|A ''tender'', puling, nice, chitty-fac'd squall 'tis. {{right|''Middleton'', More Dissemblers besides Women, iii. 1.}}}} 11. Fresh; immature; feeble; young and inexperienced. {{smaller block|For ''tendere'' wittes wenen al be wyle Ther as they kan nat pleynly understonde. {{right|''Chaucer'', Troilus, ii. 271.}}}} {{smaller block|There came two Springals, of full ''tender'' yeares. {{right|''Spenser'', F. Q., V. x. 6.}}}} {{smaller block|He left, in his ''tender'' youth, the bosom of home, of happiness, of wealth, and of rank, to plunge in the dust and blood of our inauspicious struggle. {{right|''E. Everett'', Orations, I. 465.}}}} 12†. Precious; dear. {{smaller block|I love Valentine, Whose life's as ''tender'' to me as my soul. {{right|''Shak.'', T. G. of V., v. 4. 37.}}}} 13. Careful; solicitous; considerate; watchful; concerned; unwilling to pain or injure; scrupulous: with ''of'' or ''over''. {{smaller block|So ''tender over'' his occasions, true, So feat, so nurse-like. {{right|''Shak.'', Cymbeline, v. 5. 87.}}}} {{smaller block|As this is soft and pliant to your arms In a circumferent flexure, so will I Be ''tender of'' your welfare and your will. {{right|''Chapman'', Gentleman Usher, iv.}}}} {{smaller block|Get once a good Name, and be very ''tender of'' it afterwards. {{right|''Howell'', Letters, ii. 14.}}}} {{smaller block|Don't be so ''tender'' at making an enemy now and then. {{right|''Emerson'', Conduct of Life.}}}} 14. Delicate; ticklish; apt to give pain if inconsiderately or roughly dealt with or referred to; requiring careful handling so as not to annoy or give pain: as, a ''tender'' subject. {{smaller block|In things that are ''tender'' and unpleasing, it is good to break the ice by some whose words are of less weight, and to reserve the more weighty voice to come in as by chance.{{right|''Bacon'', Cunning (ed. 1887).}}}} 15†. Quick; keen; sharp. {{smaller block|The full-fed hound or gorged hawk,
Unapt for ''tender'' smell or speedy flight.{{right|''Shak.'', Lucrece, l. 695.}}}} 16. Of ships, apt to lean over under sail; tender-sided: same as ''crank''4, 1.—17†. Yielding to a small force; sensitive. {{smaller block|These, being weighed in a pair of ''tender'' scales, amounted to one grain and a quarter.{{right|''Boyle'', Subtilty of Effluviums, ii.}}}} '''Tender porcelain.''' {{smaller|See ''porcelain''1.}} II.† ''n.'' A tender regard; fondness; affection; regard. {{smaller block|Thou hast redeem'd thy lost opinion,
And show'd thou makest some ''tender'' of my life.{{right|''Shak.'', 1 Hen. IV., v. 4. 49.}}}} {{smaller block|I had a kind of a ''Tender'' for Dolly.{{right|''Mrs. Centlivre'', The Man's Bewitched, v. 2.}}}} {{smaller block|I swear, Lady Harriot, were I not already yours, I could have a ''Tender'' for this Lady. {{right|''Steele'', Grief A-la-Mode, v. 1.}}}} '''tender'''1 (ten′dėr), ''v. t.'' [ME. ''tendren''; < ''tender''1, ''a.''] 1†. To regard or treat with compassion, solicitude, fondness, or care; cherish; hence, to hold dear; value; esteem. {{smaller block|Wherfor I besech yow of yowr faderly pyte to ''tendre'' the more thys symple wryghtyng, as I schal owt of dowght her after doo that schal please yow to the uttermest of my power and labor.{{right|''Paston Letters'', I. 436.}}}} {{smaller block|Your minion, whom . . . I ''tender'' dearly.{{right|''Shak.'', T. N., v. 1. 129.}}}} {{smaller block|As you ''tender'' your Ears, be secret. {{right|''Congreve'', Way of the World, i. 2.}}}} {{smaller block|I saw anothers fate approaching fast, And left mine owne his safetie to ''tender''. {{right|''Spenser'', Virgil's Gnat, l. 362.}}}} {{smaller block|What of the ravenous Tygre then, To lose her yong she ''tender'd'' with such care? {{right|''Heywood'', Dialogues (Works, ed. Pearson, 1874, VI. 136).}}}} 2. To make tender, in any sense. {{smaller block|I pray God forgive you, open your eyes, ''tender'' your hearts. {{right|''Penn'', To J. H., etc.}}}} {{smaller block|If too strongly acid or alkaline it [the mordant] will have a corrosive action, and the goods, as it is technically called, will be ''tendered''. {{right|''W. Crookes'', Dyeing and Calico-Printing, p. 517.}}}} '''tender'''2 (ten′dėr), ''v.'' [< F. ''tendre'' = Pr. ''tendre'' = Sp. Pg. ''tender'' = It. ''tendere'', stretch, display, also tender, offer, < L. ''tendere'', stretch, extend: see ''tend''1. ''Tender'', like ''render'', ''surrender'', retains, exceptionally, the termination of the F. inf.; ''tend''1 is the same word without this termination.] I. ''trans.'' 1. To offer; make offer of; present for acceptance: as, to ''tender'' one a complimentary dinner; to ''tender'' one's resignation. {{smaller block|Most mighty Lord (quoth Adam), heer I ''tender'' All thanks I can, not all I should thee render. {{right|''Sylvester'', tr. of Du Bartas's Weeks, ii., Eden.}}}} {{smaller block|Upon ''tendring'' my Present, he seemed to smile, and gave me a gentle Nod. {{right|''Bailey'', tr. of Colloquies of Erasmus, II. 2.}}}}
